items.title: Restaurant chain's direct ordering website with kitchen display
items.body:
CLIENT: Company A, Hyderabad. Biryani and Hyderabadi food chain with 14 outlets and 3 cloud kitchens. 520 staff, revenue ₹90–105 crore a year, 55% of it through food delivery apps.

TODAY: Delivery apps charge 25–30% in commission and fees. A phone line takes bulk and party orders. Each outlet's billing system is separate, menus and prices are updated by hand on every app, and the brand owns no customer data. Kitchens work from printed tickets.

THE PROBLEM: Assumptions: app sales are 55% of ₹96 crore = ₹52.8 crore at 27% average commission. Moving 12% of that to direct orders, where delivery and payment costs are 12%, saves 15 points on ₹6.336 crore = ₹95.04 lakh. The phone line loses 30 bulk orders a month at ₹18,000 and 30% margin: 30 × ₹5,400 × 12 = ₹19.44 lakh. Total ₹1.14 crore a year.

USERS: Customers (mobile), outlet managers and kitchen staff, and the central marketing team. The founder-CEO signs the deal.

THE ASK: I pay the apps a quarter of every order and they own my customers. I want our own ordering site that is faster and nicer than the apps, with one menu and prices I control. Orders should go straight to the right outlet's kitchen screen. Regulars should earn rewards for ordering direct, and party orders should be easy to place.

MUST HAVE:
- Ordering web app: outlet picked by location and delivery radius, menu with photos, add-ons and portions, cart, coupons, UPI and card payment (test mode), and live order status
- Central menu CMS: items, prices by city, outlet availability, time-based menus, photos, veg and non-veg marks, spice level
- Kitchen display per outlet: new orders with timers, prep stages, ready for pickup, and rider handoff
- Loyalty points on direct orders, redeemed at checkout
- Party order form with minimum notice and confirmation by the catering manager
- Dashboard of orders, prep time, cancellations and repeat customers by outlet

CORE BUILD: Software Engineering candidates must ship this slice end to end, in about 6 to 8 screens: ordering web app with menu and cart, test payment, central menu admin, and outlet kitchen display. Roles: customer and kitchen staff. AI: prep-time estimate. Hard part: real-time order updates on the kitchen screen. Mock payments, messages and outside systems, and seed from the sample data. The rest of MUST HAVE is optional depth.

OUT OF SCOPE:
- Delivery app integration
- An own rider app (riders come from a delivery partner)
- Replacing outlet billing or inventory

AI OR AUTOMATION: Orders route to the right outlet automatically, status updates go out by WhatsApp or SMS, and items pause when an outlet marks them out of stock. AI suggests reorders from each customer's history and predicts prep time from current kitchen load, so the promised time is honest. When it is wrong: suggestions never add items to the cart; the promised time is the higher of the AI estimate and the outlet's minimum; an order 10 minutes past its promise alerts the outlet manager and updates the customer; managers can override estimates.

CONSTRAINTS: Show each outlet's FSSAI licence number, veg and non-veg symbols and allergens. Prices include 5% GST and must say so. Customer data is personal data under the DPDP Act 2023; marketing messages need opt-in. Friday and Sunday dinner peaks reach 1,200 orders an hour across outlets. Kitchens use cheap Android tablets in hot, noisy spaces.

DESIGN: The client values good, minimal design: clean layouts, white space, a restrained palette and clear type, with nothing on screen that lacks a purpose. Design counts as much as features. The menu should make people hungry: big food photos, a short scannable menu, easy-to-read prices and checkout in under a minute. The kitchen screen must be readable from two metres, with colour marking late orders.

BUDGET AND TIME: ₹9 lakh, 8 weeks. Success: direct orders equal to 12% of app orders within 9 months; median checkout under 60 seconds; 35% of direct customers ordering again within a month by month 6.

items.title: Pharmacy chain's online reordering with pharmacist prescription checks
items.body:
CLIENT: Company A, Kolkata. Pharmacy chain with 46 stores across Kolkata and Howrah and a central warehouse. 380 staff, revenue ₹180–210 crore a year, with a large share from repeat medicines for diabetes, blood pressure and thyroid.

TODAY: Customers call or WhatsApp a store with a photo of their prescription. Pharmacists check stock and reply, and staff deliver locally. Refills depend on customers remembering. Prescriptions sit on store phones, and stores cannot see each other's stock.

THE PROBLEM: Assumptions: 9,000 regular customers spend ₹2,200 a month each. Each month 20% (1,800) skip or buy elsewhere because nobody reminded them or their store was out of stock: 1,800 × ₹2,200 = ₹39.6 lakh of sales × 18% margin = ₹7.13 lakh a month, ₹85.54 lakh a year. WhatsApp orders: 600 a day × 6 minutes = 60 hours × 360 days × ₹220 = ₹47.52 lakh. Total ₹1.33 crore a year.

USERS: Customers and caregivers (mobile), store pharmacists, and central operations. The Managing Director signs the deal.

THE ASK: My regular customers should reorder their monthly medicines in a minute and get them the same day from the nearest store with stock. A pharmacist must check the prescription every time, with nothing slipping through. Remind customers before they run out. I want one view of orders across all 46 stores.

MUST HAVE:
- Customer web app: OTP login, family profiles, search, prescription upload, cart, refill subscriptions, UPI and cash on delivery (test mode), order tracking
- Pharmacist verification queue: prescription beside the matched items, with approve, edit or reject with reason
- Routing to the nearest store with stock, from a daily stock CSV
- Refill reminders from quantity and dosage, with one-tap reorder
- Store order screen: pick, pack, store invoice number and handover to delivery
- Central dashboard: orders by store, verification time and rejections

CORE BUILD: Software Engineering candidates must ship this slice end to end, in about 6 to 8 screens: reorder flow with prescription upload, pharmacist verification queue, store routing, and refill reminders. Roles: customer and pharmacist. AI: prescription reading as a draft. Hard part: blocking Schedule H items without approval. Mock payments, messages and outside systems, and seed from the sample data. The rest of MUST HAVE is optional depth.

OUT OF SCOPE:
- Doctor consultations
- Lab test booking
- Integration with store billing software

AI OR AUTOMATION: AI reads uploaded prescriptions, often handwritten, and suggests matching products and quantities, plus cheaper generic options. When it is wrong: AI output is only a draft in the pharmacist's queue, and a registered pharmacist approves every item; unreadable ones get a re-upload request; generic options need pharmacist approval and customer consent; the system never gives medical advice.

CONSTRAINTS: Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules, Schedule H and H1 medicines need a valid prescription; Schedule X and narcotic items must not be sold online at all; H1 sales need a register with prescriber and patient details. Online pharmacy rules are not final, so keep rules configurable. Prescriptions are sensitive health data under the DPDP Act 2023: encrypt them and log access. Bengali, Hindi and English.

DESIGN: The client values good, minimal design: clean layouts, white space, a restrained palette and clear type, with nothing on screen that lacks a purpose. Design counts as much as features. Customers are often worried or ordering for a parent: the app must feel calm and trustworthy, with large text, a clear reorder button on the home screen and no promotional clutter. Pharmacists should compare the prescription and matched items side by side.

BUDGET AND TIME: ₹9 lakh, 8 weeks. Success: 30% of regular customers ordering online in 6 months; monthly drop-off from 20% to 10%; median verification under 10 minutes; no Schedule H or H1 item dispatched without approval.
